column1: Learning a baseline of normal behavior and flagging deviations is anomaly/behavior-based detection. Signature-based filtering matches known patterns, hashing protects stored passwords, and physical access control governs entry to spaces.
Which are legitimate ways AI helps defenders?
I.   Detecting unusual account behavior faster than manual review
II.  Triaging large volumes of alerts to surface likely threats
III. Guaranteeing zero false positives in threat detection

AI excels at rapidly spotting anomalies (I) and prioritizing high volumes of alerts (II). Statement III is false: AI systems still produce false positives and false negatives and cannot guarantee perfect accuracy.
Which statement BEST describes a key limitation of relying on AI for cyber defense?
• A AI defenses make human oversight completely unnecessary
• B AI defenses can produce false positives and may miss novel attacks not reflected in their training
• C AI defenses can detect only attacks that have already been publicly reported
• D AI defenses cannot process more data than a human analyst
Answer: B. AI defenses can produce false positives and may miss novel attacks not reflected in their training

AI defenses can misclassify benign activity (false positives) and may fail on truly novel attacks outside their learned patterns, so human oversight remains important. They do process more data than humans and are not limited to publicly reported attacks.

column1: Why is human review still important even when AI handles most threat detection?
• A Humans can read encrypted traffic that AI cannot
• B AI is unable to process more than one alert at a time
• C Humans never make mistakes in security decisions
• D Humans can investigate flagged events in context and catch AI errors
Answer: D. Humans can investigate flagged events in context and catch AI errors

Humans add contextual judgment and can correct AI mistakes such as false positives or missed novel attacks. AI handles high volume well, neither humans nor AI read properly encrypted traffic without keys, and humans are certainly not error-free.

A website becomes unreachable because thousands of compromised devices flood it with traffic simultaneously. This attack is BEST described as:

Overwhelming a target with traffic from many distributed compromised hosts is a DDoS attack, which harms availability. A MITM intercepts traffic, SQL injection targets databases, and phishing manipulates people.
On an unencrypted network, an attacker captures and reads packets passing across the wire, including a plaintext login. This passive technique is called:
Capturing and reading network traffic is packet sniffing/eavesdropping, a passive attack. DoS disrupts availability, ARP poisoning manipulates address mappings, and brute force guesses credentials.
An attacker forges the source IP address of packets so they appear to come from a trusted internal host. This technique is BEST described as:
Falsifying the source address of packets to impersonate a trusted host is IP spoofing. Phishing targets people, cross-site scripting targets web browsers, and tailgating is a physical attack.

II.  Packet sniffing of plaintext traffic

A DDoS flood (I) and physically cutting the line (III) both deny access, harming availability. Packet sniffing (II) is a passive read that threatens confidentiality, not availability.

Which wireless configuration provides the STRONGEST protection for a modern office Wi-Fi network?
• A An open network with no password
• D Hiding the SSID with no encryption
WPA3 is the current strong standard for Wi-Fi encryption. Open networks offer none, WEP is broken and easily cracked, and hiding the SSID is obscurity that provides no real encryption.
An office configures its wireless network with the settings below. Which setting is the WEAKEST security choice?
II.  Uses WEP for backward compatibility
III. Requires a strong, regularly rotated passphrase
IV. Separates guest traffic onto its own network
WEP (II) is obsolete and can be cracked in minutes, so enabling it badly weakens the network. WPA2/WPA3, strong rotated passphrases, and guest network separation are all sound choices.
A written policy requiring employees to connect personal devices only to a separate guest network is an example of which control category?
Policies and procedures are managerial/administrative controls. The firewall or VLAN that enforces the separation would be a technical control, but the policy itself is administrative.

I.   It is a form of security through obscurity
II.  It replaces the need for encryption

Hiding an SSID is obscurity (I) and can be uncovered by attackers monitoring traffic (III). It does NOT replace encryption (II)

column1: A retailer wants to protect customer payment data on its network. Which combination BEST reflects layered network defense?
• A Place payment systems on the open guest Wi-Fi for convenience
• B Rely solely on hiding the payment server'
• C Put payment systems on an isolated segment, encrypt their traffic, and restrict access with firewall rules
• D Disable all logging to reduce noise
Answer: C. Put payment systems on an isolated segment, encrypt their traffic, and restrict access with firewall rules

Isolating payment systems, encrypting their traffic, and restricting access with firewall rules combines multiple independent controls (defense in depth). Using guest Wi-Fi, relying on SSID obscurity, or disabling logging each weakens security.
A hospital places its medical devices, guest Wi-Fi, and administrative systems on separate isolated network segments. The PRIMARY security benefit is that:
• A A compromise in one segment is contained and cannot freely spread to others
• B All devices get faster internet speeds
• C Encryption is no longer necessary
• D Passwords never need to be changed
Answer: A. A compromise in one segment is contained and cannot freely spread to others

Segmentation limits lateral movement, so an attacker who breaches one segment cannot easily reach others - it contains the blast radius. It is not primarily about speed, and it does not remove the need for encryption or password hygiene.
A company places its public web server in a DMZ between the internet and its internal network. The MAIN purpose of the DMZ is to:
• A Give the web server direct, unrestricted access to internal databases
• B Encrypt all internal email automatically
• C Replace the need for a firewall
• D Expose a public service while keeping the internal network isolated if that service is compromised
Answer: D. Expose a public service while keeping the internal network isolated if that service is compromised

A DMZ isolates internet-facing services so that compromising them does not directly expose the internal network. It deliberately restricts access into the internal zone, relies on firewalls rather than replacing them, and is unrelated to email encryption.
Which statements about network segmentation are TRUE?
I.   VLANs can logically separate traffic on shared physical hardware
II.  Segmentation can limit how far an attacker moves laterally
III. Segmentation makes encryption of sensitive data unnecessary
VLANs provide logical separation on shared switches (I) and segmentation restricts lateral movement (II). It does NOT replace encryption (III)

A firewall is configured so that all traffic is blocked unless a rule explicitly permits it. This configuration is BEST described as:
Blocking everything except explicitly permitted traffic is a default-deny (deny-by-default) policy, the more secure baseline. Default-allow permits everything not explicitly blocked

Answer: C. Option Y, because the specific deny is evaluated before the broad allow
With first-match evaluation, the specific DENY for 10.0.0.5 must come before the broad ALLOW (Option Y). In Option X the ALLOW matches 10.0.0.5 first, so the later DENY never applies.

Answer: B. It filters traffic between networks based on a set of rules
A firewall enforces rules that permit or block traffic between networks or hosts. It does not proofread email, encrypt stored files, or control physical entry.

Firewalls filter by ports/addresses (I) and a bad allow rule can admit attacks (II). No single control guarantees the network can never be breached (III)

""text"": ""Packet sniffing (eavesdropping). Capturing and reading network traffic is packet sniffing/eavesdropping, a passive attack. DoS disrupts availability, ARP poisoning manipulates address mappings, and brute force guesses credentials.""
""text"": ""An attacker forges the source IP address of packets so they appear to come from a trusted internal host. This technique is BEST described as:"",

""text"": ""IP spoofing. Falsifying the source address of packets to impersonate a trusted host is IP spoofing. Phishing targets people, cross-site scripting targets web browsers, and tailgating is a physical attack.""

""text"": ""Which of the following primarily threaten network AVAILABILITY?

I.   A DDoS flood against a server
II.  Packet sniffing of plaintext traffic
III. Cutting the fiber line to a building"",

""text"": ""I and III only. A DDoS flood (I) and physically cutting the line (III) both deny access, harming availability. Packet sniffing (II) is a passive read that threatens confidentiality, not availability.""

""text"": ""On a local network, an attacker sends forged ARP replies so that other devices associate the gateway's IP with the attacker's MAC address, routing victims' traffic through the attacker first. This enables which attack?"",

""text"": ""A man-in-the-middle attack via ARP poisoning. ARP poisoning maps a legitimate IP to the attacker's MAC, inserting the attacker into the traffic path for a man-in-the-middle attack. The other options describe database, credential, and Wi-Fi portal attacks.""
""text"": ""An attacker captures a valid authentication message and later retransmits it unchanged to gain access, without ever knowing the password. This is BEST described as:"",

""text"": ""A replay attack. Recording a valid transmission and resending it to be reauthenticated is a replay attack. It does not require knowing the credential, unlike a dictionary attack, and is unrelated to phishing or DoS.""
""text"": ""Which wireless configuration provides the STRONGEST protection for a modern office Wi-Fi network?"",

""text"": ""WPA3 encryption. WPA3 is the current strong standard for Wi-Fi encryption. Open networks offer none, WEP is broken and easily cracked, and hiding the SSID is obscurity that provides no real encryption.""
""text"": ""An office configures its wireless network with the settings below. Which setting is the WEAKEST security choice?"",

""text"": ""Setting II. WEP (II) is obsolete and can be cracked in minutes, so enabling it badly weakens the network. WPA2/WPA3, strong rotated passphrases, and guest network separation are all sound choices.""
""text"": ""A written policy requiring employees to connect personal devices only to a separate guest network is an example of which control category?"",

""text"": ""Managerial (administrative) control. Policies and procedures are managerial/administrative controls. The firewall or VLAN that enforces the separation would be a technical control, but the policy itself is administrative.""

""text"": ""Which statements about hiding a Wi-Fi network's SSID are TRUE?

I.   It is a form of security through obscurity
II.  It replaces the need for encryption
III. Determined attackers can still discover a hidden SSID"",
""text"": ""I and III only. Hiding an SSID is obscurity (I) and can be uncovered by attackers monitoring traffic (III). It does NOT replace encryption (II)
column2: a hidden network without encryption is still readable.""

""text"": ""A compromise in one segment is contained and cannot freely spread to others. It is not primarily about speed, and it does not remove the need for encryption or password hygiene.""
""text"": ""A company places its public web server in a DMZ between the internet and its internal network. The MAIN purpose of the DMZ is to:"",

""text"": ""Expose a public service while keeping the internal network isolated if that service is compromised. ""text"": ""Which statements about network segmentation are TRUE?

""text"": ""A firewall is configured so that all traffic is blocked unless a rule explicitly permits it. This configuration is BEST described as:"",

""text"": ""Default-deny. Blocking everything except explicitly permitted traffic is a default-deny (deny-by-default) policy, the more secure baseline. Default-allow permits everything not explicitly blocked
""text"": ""A firewall evaluates rules top to bottom and applies the first match. The intent is to block host 10.0.0.5 but allow the rest of 10.0.0.0/24. Which rule order achieves the intent?"",

""text"": ""Option Y, because the specific deny is evaluated before the broad allow. With first-match evaluation, the specific DENY for 10.0.0.5 must come before the broad ALLOW (Option Y). In Option X the ALLOW matches 10.0.0.5 first, so the later DENY never applies.""
""text"": ""Which statement BEST describes what a network firewall does?"",

""text"": ""It filters traffic between networks based on a set of rules. A firewall enforces rules that permit or block traffic between networks or hosts. It does not proofread email, encrypt stored files, or control physical entry.""

""text"": ""Which statements about firewalls are TRUE?

column2: an IPS can also actively block it. An IDS monitors and alerts on suspicious activity, while an IPS additionally takes action to block or drop malicious traffic in line. Neither is defined by encryption or by wired/wireless medium.""

column2: it may miss brand-new attacks not yet in its database. Matching traffic to known patterns is signature-based detection, whose weakness is missing novel (zero-day) attacks absent from its signature database. Anomaly-based detection instead learns a baseline and flags deviations.""

column1: ""text"": ""A SIEM system aggregates logs from firewalls, servers, and IDS sensors, then correlates events to highlight likely incidents. Its PRIMARY value is that it:"",

""text"": ""Centralizes and correlates data from many sources to reveal patterns a single log would miss. A SIEM centralizes and correlates events across many sources so that distributed attack patterns become visible. ""text"": ""Which statements about detecting network attacks are TRUE?

I.   Signature-based detection struggles with zero-day attacks
II.  Anomaly-based detection can generate false positives from unusual but benign activity
III. A SIEM helps correlate events from multiple devices"",

""text"": ""I, II, and III. Signature detection misses unknown attacks (I), anomaly detection can flag harmless oddities as false positives (II), and a SIEM correlates multi-source events (III). All three statements are true.""

""text"": ""A SIEM correlates these near-simultaneous events: hundreds of failed logins on a server, one success, then a large outbound data transfer to an unfamiliar IP. The MOST likely interpretation is:"",

""text"": ""A successful brute-force/guessing attack followed by data exfiltration. ""text"": ""An organization's network-monitoring setup is described below. Which gap MOST undermines its ability to detect attacks?"",

""text"": ""Gap III. If no one reviews the alerts or logs (III), detection produces no response and attacks proceed unnoticed. Watching inbound traffic, feeding logs to a SIEM, and automated correlation are all strengths, not gaps.""
""text"": ""Why does anomaly-based network detection require establishing a baseline of normal activity first?"",

""text"": ""To know what 'unusual' looks like so deviations can be flagged. Anomaly detection flags deviations from normal, so it must first learn what normal looks like. It is not an encryption, firewall, or physical-security mechanism.""

""text"": ""Traffic comes from many distributed sources, so simply blocking one address is insufficient. DDoS traffic originates from many distributed hosts, so blocking a single source does little

Dismissing it as normal, a backup, or routine ignores a clear red flag.""

""text"": ""Which signals could indicate an attack against an application or its data?

I.   A spike in database errors matching injection-style input
II.  A WAF logging many blocked malicious requests from one source
III. A routine, scheduled software update being applied"",

""text"": ""I and II only. A burst of injection-style errors (I) and many blocked malicious requests from one source (II) indicate attack activity. A scheduled software update (III) is normal maintenance, not an attack signal.""
""text"": ""An application's monitoring is configured as below. Which choice MOST weakens the ability to detect data attacks?"",

""text"": ""Choice III. Disabling logging on the most sensitive table (III) creates a blind spot exactly where attacks would be most damaging. Logging access, alerting on large exports, and reviewing WAF alerts all aid detection.""
""text"": ""Which combination BEST reflects defense in depth for protecting a sensitive customer database?"",

""text"": ""Encrypt the data at rest, enforce least-privilege access, validate application input, and log/monitor access. Combining encryption, least-privilege access control, input validation, and monitoring layers independent controls so no single failure exposes the data. A lone password, obscurity, or a single firewall with no logging are all single points of failure.""
""text"": ""Which cryptographic tool is the RIGHT choice to verify that a downloaded file was not altered in transit, without needing to keep it secret?"",

""text"": ""A published hash (checksum) of the file. Comparing a freshly computed hash to a trusted published checksum verifies integrity without secrecy. A Wi-Fi password, CPU speed, and monitor size are unrelated to verifying file integrity.""

""text"": ""Which measures help defend a web app against injection attacks?

I.   Parameterized queries that separate code from data
II.  Validating input against strict expected formats
III. Trusting all input that comes from logged-in users"",

""text"": ""I and II only. Parameterized queries (I) and strict input validation (II) defend against injection. Trusting input merely because a user is logged in (III) is unsafe, since authenticated users can also send malicious input.""
""text"": ""Why should organizations periodically review who has access to sensitive data?"",

""text"": ""To remove access that is no longer needed and catch over-privileged accounts. Access reviews catch lingering or excessive permissions (e.g., after role changes), enforcing least privilege over time. They are not about publishing data, deleting databases, or disabling encryption.""
""text"": ""A company encrypts its backups but stores the only copy of the decryption key on the same server as the backups, with no other copy. What is the MAIN risk?"",

""text"": ""If that server is lost or its key is stolen, the encryption is either useless or the data becomes unrecoverable. Co-locating the sole key with the encrypted data means an attacker who reaches the server gets both, and losing the server destroys the only key, making data unrecoverable - both reflect poor key management. The other options are nonsensical.""
""text"": ""A valid digital signature on a contract provides non-repudiation, meaning:"",

""text"": ""The signer cannot credibly deny having signed it, since only their private key could produce the signature. Because only the signer holds the private key used to sign, a valid signature ties the action to them, so they cannot plausibly deny it - that is non-repudiation. A signature authenticates and protects integrity
column2: it does not conceal the document's contents.""

""text"": ""A records system uses the access rules below. Which rule violates least privilege?"",

""text"": ""An app is vulnerable to cross-site scripting. Which fix MOST directly addresses it?"",

""text"": ""An immutable audit trail of who accessed or changed sensitive data is valuable because it:"",

""text"": ""Supports accountability and helps reconstruct what happened during an incident. A tamper-resistant audit trail provides accountability and an investigative record after an incident. It does not by itself prevent attacks, encrypt traffic, or replace access controls.""

""text"": ""An analyst relies only on cryptographic hash checks to detect attacks on a sensitive file. Which attack would this method FAIL to detect?"",

""text"": ""An attacker copies and exfiltrates the file without changing it. Hash comparison only reveals whether data have been altered. Modifying, appending, and encrypting all change the file, so the recomputed hash would not match. Copying the file leaves it byte-for-byte identical, so the hash still matches even though the data were stolen. This is the classic false negative for hash-based integrity monitoring, and it is why hashing is paired with access logging or DLP.""
